metadata.summary: Background: The molecular mechanisms underlying heart failure (HF) following myocardial infarction (MI) (HF-MI) remain incompletely understood, and whole-transcriptome profiling studies hold significant promise for disease prevention and treatment. Methods: Whole-transcriptome sequencing was performed on post-MI patients with and without HF to analyze differentially expressed mRNAs, lncRNAs, and circRNAs, along with functional enrichment analysis. Co-expression networks linking lncRNA-mRNA and circRNA-mRNA pairs, as well as ceRNA networks involving lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA and circRNA-miRNA-mRNA interactions, were constructed for differentially expressed (DE) RNAs. Key lncRNAs were validated by RT-qPCR. Transcriptional factor-lncRNA networks were constructed, and key relationships were verified using RIP-PCR. Results: Patients with HF-MI exhibited marked elevation of NT-proBNP and significant reduction in LVEF%. Transcriptome-wide analysis revealed 228 DE-mRNAs, 700 DE-lncRNAs, and 1188 DE-circRNAs in HF-MI compared to non-heart failure patients (NHF-MI). Construction of the ceRNA network identified hsa-miR-6089 and hsa-miR-6771-5p as key miRNAs in the lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA network, while hsa-miR-1207-5p and hsa-miR-10392-3p were key miRNAs in the circRNA-miRNA-mRNA network. PVT1, SNHG5, TTN-AS1, HCP5, and OIP5-AS1 were identified as the five key DE-lncRNAs, with PVT1/SNHG5 showing upregulation and TTN-AS1/HCP5/OIP5-AS1 exhibiting downregulation. The transcription factor-lncRNA network primarily involves GLIS3-HCP5 and ZNF135-PVT1, with validated associative interactions. Conclusion: This study systematically mapped the regulatory network of HF-MI, revealing the roles of the GLIS3-HCP5 and ZNF135-PVT1 regulatory axes in HF-MI, thereby providing a basis for exploring novel therapeutic strategies.

observations.title: Transcriptome Expression Profiles and Regulatory Networks in Patients with Heart Failure Following Myocardial Infarction

observations.text:
ObjectivesPublicly available datasets for clinical speech de-identification remain scarce due to privacy constraints and annotation complexity. We address this gap with the 2025 SREDH/AI Cup SHI Speech Corpus, a time-aligned clinical speech dataset for detecting sensitive health information (SHI).

MethodsThe dataset integrates three sources: the OpenDeID-v2 corpus, the dataset for automated medical transcription and medical dialogues derived from Taiwanese television dramas, combining English medical speech with Mandarin Chinese utterances. All audio was manually annotated with millisecond-level, time-aligned SHI segments using a schema of eight primary categories and 38 subcategories of which 26 were attested.

ResultsThe corpus comprises approximately 20 hours of annotated audio (19.36 hours English, 0.89 hours Chinese) and 7830 SHI entities, split into training (10 hours, 1539 files), validation (5 hours, 775 files) and test (5 hours, 710 files) sets, supporting evaluation of both automatic speech recognition (ASR) and SHI recognition. Interannotator agreement (Fleisss kappa) reached 0.907. In the 2025 SREDH/AI Cup competition, top-performing systems achieved a mixed error rate of 0.1147 in ASR and a macro F1 of 0.7103 in SHI recognition.

DiscussionSHI category distribution is long-tailed, and English-Chinese data volume is highly imbalanced, underscoring the scarcity of Chinese clinical speech resources and the difficulty of time-aligned annotation in low-resource settings.

ConclusionThis corpus approximates dialogue-based clinical scenarios and supports research on medical speech de-identification, offering a unique reference for low-resource clinical speech privacy protection.

Key messageO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABS- Publicly available clinical speech datasets containing time-aligned sensitive health information (SHI) annotations for clinical speech de-identification research are limited.


What this study adds- The 2025 SREDH AI Cup SHI Speech Corpus introduces a clinically oriented speech dataset with millisecond-level time-aligned SHI annotations covering 26 of the 38 SHI subcategories defined in the annotation schema.
- The corpus integrates structured annotation protocols and standardized data processing to support the reproducible benchmarking of speech-based de-identification models.


How this study might affect research, practice or policy- The availability of time-aligned SHI annotations may facilitate research on real-time or streaming de-identification systems beyond conventional, transcription-focused approaches.
- This dataset may support the development of privacy-preserving technologies for clinical speech in bilingual settings involving English and low-resource languages.

observations.text: The contribution of pre-existing smooth muscle cell (SMC) states to vascular lesions remains unresolved. Here we identify a rare, progenitor-like Primed SMC compartment before lesion formation in sham-operated carotid arteries and across Myh11-lineage marked mouse aortic datasets, with a Primed-like counterpart in non-diseased human aorta. Primed SMCs retain SMC identity while combining attenuated contractile programmes with conserved niche-associated (Cd34, Fst, Tnfrsf11b) and matricellular (Vcam1, Thbs1, Timp1) cores, overlaid by vessel-specific developmental signatures (Nrn1, Gdf10, Scx). After carotid ligation and during high-fat diet-induced atherosclerosis in Ldlr-/- and Apoe-/- mice, disease-associated Primed, cycling and fibrochondrocyte populations preferentially map to baseline Primed SMCs, whereas contractile SMCs are depleted as inferred feeder sources. Concordant trajectory, graph-based and cross-dataset analyses support a model in which this pre-existing compartment is the dominant inferred source of SMC-derived lesional cellularity. These findings favour expansion and diversification of the Primed compartment over widespread phenotypic switching of contractile SMCs.
observations.title: A rare pre-existing progenitor-like Primed SMC compartment is the dominant inferred source of SMC-derived cellularity in vascular injury and atherosclerosis

observations.text:
BackgroundBurn injuries disproportionately affect resource-limited settings. India alone reports over seven million burn injuries annually against only 67 dedicated burn centres. Consequently, initial assessments, such as total burn surface area (%TBSA), which directly influence fluid resuscitation and referral decisions, are frequently performed by non-specialist staff, with known inter-observer variability. Existing computer-assisted tools either require manual annotation on a generic 3D body model or estimate %TBSA using an anatomical approximation (the Rule of Nines) rather than from the patients own segmented body area.

MethodsWe developed BurnCare, a deployable artificial intelligence-assisted web and Android-based platform that estimates %TBSA from a single smartphone photograph. The pipeline was developed as a two-stage deep learning system that first isolated the patient from the background (ResNet50 encoder, U-Net decoder) and then segmented the burn skin within that region (DenseNet169 encoder, U-Net decoder), with both stages trained on a prospectively collected, multi-device dataset from a tertiary burn centre in India. The platform supports %TBSA estimation both with scale calibration -- using a surgical tape of known length -- and without it. %TBSA estimated using BurnCare was compared with independent, blinded estimates from three healthcare professionals for 16 patient photographs, using Pearsons correlation coefficient, mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE) and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).

ResultsThe background-removal and burn-segmentation models achieved strong performance (intersection over union 0.9811 and 0.8504, respectively). BurnCares automatic %TBSA estimate correlated strongly with the mean of three clinicians estimates (r = 0.746, p < 0.001, MAE = 6.29, RMSE = 8.63 percentage points; n = 16), improving to r = 0.853 (MAE = 4.32, RMSE = 6.37) after manual mask correction; the ICC among the three clinicians alone was 0.728.

ConclusionsA two-stage artificial intelligence-assisted platform, BurnCare, was developed. The platform supports burn detection and %TBSA using deep learning models trained on real-world patient datasets. The foreground prediction is supported by a hybrid ResNet50-U-Net, while burn skin prediction is supported by a DenseNet169-U-Net. BurnCares %TBSA estimates agree with clinical judgement about as closely as clinicians agree with each other, supporting its use as a decision-support and documentation tool for burn triage in resource-limited settings. The dataset collected and the BurnCare platform are available online.
observations.title: BurnCare: A deep learning framework for burn injury assessment and TBSA estimation.

BackgroundHigher resting or sleeping heart rate (HR) has been associated with poorer glucose metabolism in adults without diabetes. However, these associations were estimated across individuals, and within-person characterization of this co-regulation during naturalistic sleep in large free-living cohorts remains limited.

ObjectiveThis study aimed to determine whether average sleeping HR, an indirect index of cardiac autonomic tone, is associated with nocturnal glucose within a participant and between participants, and whether night-to-night irregularity in sleep duration, sleep onset, and wake time is associated with nocturnal glycemia.

MethodsIn this retrospective observational study, adults who concurrently wore an Ultrahuman Ring and a continuous glucose monitor between January 2024 and June 2025 were analyzed. After participant- and night-level filtering, the cohort comprised 2648 participants from 87 countries, contributing 105,196 paired nights. Each predictor was decomposed into within- and between-participant components by person-mean centering and entered a single linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept for participant, adjusted for age, body mass index (BMI), and sex. Outcomes were nocturnal mean glucose, nocturnal glucose coefficient of variation (CV), and nocturnal time in range (70-110 mg/dL). Per-participant slopes were fitted in participants with sustained wear (at least 30 nights spanning at least 60 days). Estimates were re-derived under trimming and robust-regression specifications and refitted within BMI and regional strata.

ResultsHigher average sleeping HR was associated with higher nocturnal mean glucose both within participants (+5.7 mg/dL per 10 bpm, 95% CI 5.4-5.9) and between participants (+6.5 mg/dL, 95% CI 5.6-7.3; both P<.001). Within participants, higher sleeping HR was also associated with higher glucose CV (+1.37 percentage points, 95% CI 1.30-1.43) and lower time in range (-6.3 percentage points, 95% CI -6.7 to -6.0). Of the 911 sustained-wear participants, 701 (76.9%, 95% CI 74.1%-79.6%) had a positive individual slope (median of +5.2 mg/dL per 10 bpm). The association survived in every BMI stratum and in all 5 regional strata. Sleep-duration irregularity was associated with mean glucose between participants (+4.1 mg/dL per 30 minutes, 95% CI 2.6-5.7) but only weakly within them (+0.23 mg/dL). Within participants, a night 1 standard deviation above a participants own mean sleeping HR corresponded to 2.5 mg/dL higher nocturnal mean glucose.

ConclusionsAverage sleeping HR was associated with glucose within individuals as well as between them, indicating that the relationship is not attributable solely to stable between-person differences and reflects, at least in part, night-to-night covariation. The association was modest, but discernible in naturalistic sleep across geographies. Sleep-duration irregularity was associated with nocturnal glycemia mainly between individuals.
observations.title: Between- and Within-Person Coupling of Nocturnal Heart Rate and Glucose: Retrospective, Real-World Observational Study of 105,196 Nights From 2648 Adults Using Ultrahuman Ring and Continuous Glucose Monitoring

observations.text: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is classically associated with motor control but is increasingly recognised as a key component of the neural circuits underlying cognition. However, how the STN encodes learned reward associations and updates these representations when environmental contingencies change remains unclear. Here, we combined fibre photometry calcium imaging and chemogenetic inhibition to identify the contribution of the STN in reward learning and cognitive flexibility. During established Pavlovian conditioning, calcium imaging of the STN showed distinctive responses to reward predictive cue and reward delivery, while no response was detected to unrewarded cues. Upon reversal of reward predictive cues, STN activity initially remained associated with the previously rewarded cue before remapping to the newly rewarded cue as animals acquired the updated contingency. Chemogenetic inhibition of the STN impaired cue discrimination on established Pavlovian conditioning, delayed reversal learning, and disrupted outcome-specific Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer. Together these results demonstrate that STN activity is required for flexible updating of learned reward associations and goal-directed behaviour. These findings establish the STN as a dynamic integrative hub that encodes and updates learned reward representations to support cognitive flexibility, extending its role beyond motor control to include goal-directed behaviour. We show STN activity tracks reward-predictive cues and updates when contingencies reverse. Overall, these findings demonstrate that the STN is not just downstream of cortical control but actively supports updating of reward associations.
observations.title: Subthalamic Nucleus dynamically encodes reward value and cognitive flexibility

observations.text:
BackgroundMRI-visible perivascular spaces (PVS) are an imaging marker of compromised brain health function. However, robust PVS segmentation remains challenging: conventional methods often require cohort-specific parameter tuning, while supervised deep-learning models depend on extensive manual annotations for training and may fail to generalise to unseen scanners, protocols, and clinical populations.

MethodsWe introduce DRIPS (Domain Randomisation for Image-based PVS Segmentation), a fully automated deep-learning framework trained exclusively on synthetic data. By learning PVS representations from a plethora of simulated cases, DRIPS transfers to real-world MRI without using manually labelled PVS data from real participants. We evaluated DRIPS in 185 fully manually annotated MRI scans from eight independent cohorts encompassing diverse clinical populations and acquisition settings, including 3T and 7T imaging, T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences, and isotropic and anisotropic resolutions. DRIPS was compared with five previously published methods.

ResultsAcross cohorts, DRIPS significantly outperformed the second-best method for both area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) and centreline Dice similarity coefficient (clDice), with mean gains of at least 0.1: 0.146 for basal ganglia (BG) AUPRC (P = 0.008), 0.125 for centrum semiovale (CSO) AUPRC (P = 0.008), 0.112 for BG clDice (P = 0.016), and 0.186 for CSO clDice (P = 0.008). Importantly, its performance was not associated with white matter hyperintensity burden.

ConclusionsDRIPS enables accurate, fully automated PVS segmentation across heterogeneous imaging settings without the need for real PVS annotations for training.
observations.title: DRIPS: Domain Randomisation for Image-based Perivascular spaces Segmentation

metadata.summary: This study generated a transcriptome-wide resource of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) from two clinical groups: subjects with hyperuricemia (HUA, n=15) and subjects with coronary artery disease together with hyperuricemia (CHD_HUA, n=15). Total RNA was extracted from PBMC and poly(A)+ mRNA was enriched with oligo(dT) magnetic beads. Strand-specific libraries were constructed using dUTP incorporation and UDG second-strand digestion, and paired-end 150 bp sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Clean reads were aligned to the Homo sapiens reference genome with HISAT2, and transcripts were assembled and quantified with StringTie. Gene-level raw read counts and FPKM values for all 30 samples are provided as processed data, together with the paired-end FASTQ files. The dataset is intended to support investigation of transcriptional differences between hyperuricemia and coronary artery disease with hyperuricemia.

metadata.summary: Obesity-induced metabolic cardiomyopathy features myocardial lipid overload, mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic inflammation, with few targeted therapies. Hyodeoxycholic acid (HDCA), a natural secondary bile acid, plays key roles in metabolic homeostasis, yet its direct cardioprotective effects in obesity-related cardiac injury remain unclear. Here, we investigated HDCA effects on high-fat diet-induced cardiomyopathy using in vivo, lipotoxic cardiomyocyte and 3D cardiac spheroid models. HDCA ameliorated cardiac dysfunction, hypertrophic remodeling and myocardial lipid accumulation. Transcriptomics showed HDCA remodelled cardiac programs governing mitochondrial and lipid metabolism as well as inflammation. Mechanistically, HDCA limited cardiomyocyte lipid uptake via TGR5-dependent suppression of CD36 membrane localization, boosted mitochondrial respiration and ATP production, and reduced oxidative stress. HDCA also bound PIK3CA to inhibit PI3K-AKT-mediated inflammation. In 3D cardiac spheroids, HDCA alleviated lipotoxic injury. Collectively, HDCA protects against obesity-associated cardiomyopathy by coordinating myocardial lipid metabolism, mitochondrial homeostasis and inflammatory signaling, representing a promising candidate for metabolic heart disease.

observations.title: Hyodeoxycholic acid protects against obesity-associated cardiomyopathy by restoring myocardial metabolic homeostasis and suppressing inflammatory remodeling

metadata.summary: Laminopathies comprise a diverse array of phenotypes that involve multiple organs and are caused by mutations in the LMNA gene, which encodes nuclear envelope protein lamin A (LMNA). Cardiac involvement is a prominent feature and a major cause of mortality and morbidity in laminopathies. LMNA interacts with chromatin through lamin-associated domains (LADs) and regulates gene expression. The role of the LMNA in regulating chromatin structure and gene expression in cardiac myocytes is unknown.  We conditionally deleted the Lmna gene specifically in cardiac myocytes in the mouse, isolated the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes, and characterized genomic structure and function at two levels: first, by identifying and characterizing the genome-wide CTCF binding sites by a CUT&RUN assay; and second, the chromatin conformational changes by HiC.  To determine the role of LMNA in genome organization and gene expression we integrated CTCF binding, LAD, Hi-C data with the gene expression (RNA-seq), and DNA double-stranded breaks (DSBs), determined by END-Seq, in cardiac myocytes.  Compared to wild-type (WT) myocytes, LMNA deficiency increased genomic occupancy of CTCF , predominantly outside of the constitutive LADs (cLADs), and increased gene expression at the CTCF binding sites. Likewise, DSBs were highly enriched at the CTCF binding sites. However, only a small fraction of the chromatin compartments was shifted in the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes. LMNA-deficiency changed the organization of one-third of the topologically-associated domains (TADs). The changes were characterized by the merger of 2 or more TADs (60%), mainly in the non-LAD regions, splitting (30%), and shifting boundaries (10%). Reorganization of TADs, however, did not directly affect gene expression or the prevalence of DSBs. A remarkable effect of the LMNA deficiency was on chromatin loops, as it led to a gain of ~ 600 and a loss of ~1000 loops, whose boundaries were enriched in the CTCF binding sites. The changes affected the transcript level of ~25% of the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes. The gain of the loop was associated with increased gene expression, whereas the loss of the loop had the opposite effect. A multivariate analysis showed that differential CTCF  binding  (largest), loops, and cLADs affected the transcript levels of the DEGs, whereas TADs and chromatin compartments appeared to act in concert with these factors  rather than as independent determinants.  In conclusion, LMNA regulates chromatin structure like TADs its role in  gene expression is mediated mainly through CTCF, cLADs, and loops,. The findings provide insights into the molecular pathogenesis of cardiac involvement in the diverse array of phenotypes in laminopathies.

observations.title: Effects of the Lamin A on Chromatin Structure and Function in Cardiac Myocytes in a Mouse Model of Lamin-Cardiomyopathy

metadata.summary: Truncating variants in desmoplakin (DSP) are a leading cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a severe heart muscle disease characterized by fibrosis and life-threatening arrhythmias. Desmoplakin anchors the junctions that hold heart muscle cells together to the internal cytoskeleton, enabling the heart to withstand the force of each contraction. No targeted therapy exists, and DSP is too large for conventional gene replacement. Here we show, in explanted human hearts and in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, that truncating DSP variants reduce desmoplakin RNA and protein, and that the resulting haploinsufficiency renders cardiomyocytes vulnerable to cell–cell adhesion failure under contractile stress, preceded by disruption of the cell membrane. Lowering contractile force with the myosin inhibitor mavacamten prevents this failure. Circumventing the size of DSP, CRISPR-based transcriptional activation of the endogenous gene restores desmoplakin expression and rescues adhesion. Haploinsufficiency is therefore the primary defect in DSP cardiomyopathy, and transcriptional activation offers a therapeutic strategy.

observations.title: Desmoplakin Haploinsufficiency Underlies Cell-Cell Adhesion Failure in DSP Cardiomyopathy and is Rescued by Transcriptional Activation

observations.text: Polysomnography (PSG) is central to sleep medicine, yet its analysis remains hindered by labor-intensive manual scoring and limited cross-center generalizability. We present LPSGM, a large-scale PSG model trained on 220,500 hours of data from 16 public datasets (24,000 recordings) that addresses two challenges: cross-center sleep staging generalization and PSG-based screening of narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and depression. LPSGM integrates domain-adaptive pre-training, flexible channel configurations, and a unified architecture to accommodate heterogeneous recording protocols. In prospective validation, LPSGM achieves expert-level sleep staging ({kappa} = 0.845 {+/-} 0.066 vs. inter-expert {kappa} = 0.850 {+/-} 0.102) and matches fully supervised models on independent private cohorts. For downstream screening, LPSGM achieves 84.2% accuracy ({kappa} = 0.761) in three-class narcolepsy classification, with cross-institutional transfer for normal-versus-abnormal hypersomnia yielding an AUC of 0.879. Severe OSA screening reaches an AUC of 0.874 without access to respiratory signals. Depression symptom screening achieves an AUC of 0.801 in a surrogate-labeled APPLES cohort, and cross-dataset transfer to an independent clinically diagnosed cohort reaches an AUC of 0.965. These results suggest that LPSGMs pre-trained representations capture sleep-related signatures that generalize across institutions and support PSG-based screening of clinically relevant conditions. The code and pre-trained model are publicly available at https://github.com/Deng-GuiFeng/LPSGM.
observations.title: A Unified Flexible Large Polysomnography Model for Sleep Staging and Downstream Clinical Screening

metadata.summary: Background: Reactive oxygen species are increased across most pulmonary hypertension (PH) etiologies, resulting in increased reactive lipid dicarbonyls, which form protein adducts and impair mitochondrial function. We hypothesized that reducing reactive lipids would reduce right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) and improve cardiac function by eliminating protein-lipid damage feedback loops. Methods: We used 2-hydroxybenzylamine (2-HOBA) to scavenge reactive lipids in three complimentary mouse models of PH: AKR-high fat diet (HFD, metabolic stress), LNAME-HFD (cardiometabolic syndrome), and pulmonary artery banding (PAB, load stress). Cardiac function was measured by echocardiography and catheterization. RV energy metabolism was determined by oxygraphy. Mass spectrometry analyzed lipids and ceramides; O-link and RNA-Seq evaluated proteomic and gene expression in lungs, RV, and LV. Results: Reducing reactive lipids with 2-HOBA resulted in a ~10% reduction in RVSP, reduced diastolic dysfunction, reduced plasma lipids and ceramides, and normalized RV fatty acid oxidation that was severely impaired in the AKR-HFD and PAB models. Proteomic and RNA changes in the lungs, RV, and LV suggested reduced oxidative damage and inflammatory signaling and altered developmental and actin organization signaling; these changes are plausibly associated with the improved adaptation. Some changes were sex specific, including a 4x higher cardiac fatty acid content in males than females. Conclusions: Reactive lipid scavenging improves cardiac metabolic and diastolic function and pulmonary vascular resistance through restoration of mitochondrial function and reduced oxidative protein damage. The magnitude of hemodynamic improvement combined with substantial diastolic function improvement suggests clinical potential, particularly for PH patients with metabolic comorbidities.

observations.title: Reducing Reactive Lipids Improves Cardiac Metabolic and Diastolic Function in Pulmonary Hypertension Models

metadata.summary: Background. Rheumatic heart valve disease (RHVD) is the leading cause of acquired valvular disease worldwide, driven by autoimmune responses that sustain chronic inflammation and fibrotic remodeling, predominantly affecting the mitral valve (MV). Although immune dysregulation and transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling are implicated, the molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression and their relationship to clinical severity remain incompletely defined. Methods. We performed a tissue-centric multi-omics study combining histopathology, unbiased proteomics of human MV tissue (n=72), and plasma proteomics from an external cohort (n=445). We associated proteomic signatures with clinical parameters. Cross-species validation involved single-cell RNA sequencing from a murine model of autoimmune valvular carditis. Mechanistic studies used primary human valvular interstitial cells (VICs) and a three-dimensional MV mimetics. Results. RHVD MVs exhibited leaflet thickening, fibrosis, immune cell infiltration, and neovascularization, with T-cell abundance correlating with tissue remodeling. Proteomic profiling identified 1,436 differentially expressed proteins enriched in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, immune response, hemostasis, and multi-growth factor signaling, including TGF-β and insulin-like growth factor binding protein (IGFBP) pathway. Integrated tissue-plasma analysis revealed shared molecular signatures. The mean transvalvular gradient captured the hemodynamic continuum from mitral regurgitation to stenosis and was associated with coordinated with ECM remodeling, cytoskeletal, immune, and hemostatic pathways. Cross-species integration confirmed convergence on ECM remodeling, immune activation, and TGF-β/IGFBP signaling, predominantly in VIC and myofibroblast populations. Mechanistically, TGF-β induced IGFBP5, IGFBP7, and CCN2 expression in VICs, while their silencing attenuated collagen expression. MV mimetics exposed to pro-fibrotic and inflammatory stimuli recapitulated these findings. Conclusions. TGF-β-centered signaling networks drive the coordinated immune, and fibrotic remodeling that characterizes RHVD. The TGF-β-IGFBP axis emerges as a key mediator of VIC-driven fibrosis and links molecular remodeling to clinical disease progression, highlighting novel therapeutic opportunities.

observations.title: Integrative Multimodal Analysis of Rheumatic Mitral Valve Disease Identifies Insulin‑Like Growth Factor Binding Proteins as Profibrotic Drivers

metadata.summary: Reperfusion of ischemic myocardium triggers a sterile inflammatory cascade in which NF-κB–dependent transcriptional priming precedes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation. Diacerein, approved for osteoarthritis, is converted in vivo to rhein, an NF-κB inhibitor with inflammasome-attenuating properties, but its effect on the ischemic myocardial transcriptome is unknown.  To define the transcriptional program underlying diacerein-mediated cardioprotection, male Wistar rats received oral diacerein (80 mg/kg/day) or vehicle for 10 days before the heart was isolated and subjected to global no-flow ischemia followed by reperfusion in a Langendorff preparation. RNA sequencing of left ventricular tissue identified 314 differentially expressed genes (268 downregulated, 46 upregulated) in diacerein- versus vehicle-treated hearts. Downregulated genes included Selp (P-selectin), the endothelial adhesion molecule mediating leukocyte capture, Csf2rb (the shared GM-CSF/IL-3/IL-5 receptor subunit), and Ripk1, while Card9 was upregulated. Gene set enrichment analysis showed suppression of TNF signaling, NF-κB signaling, and cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction pathways.  These data indicate that diacerein pretreatment suppresses leukocyte recruitment and inflammatory priming programs in the ischemic myocardium, and provide a transcriptional basis for its cardioprotective effect.

observations.title: Rhein attenuates myocardial ischemia–reperfusion injury by suppressing NF-κB–driven inflammatory priming

metadata.gds_type: Methylation profiling by high throughput sequencing
metadata.summary: Environmental exposures to toxic chemicals can profoundly alter the transcriptome and epigenome in both humans and animals, contributing to disease development across the lifespan. To elucidate how early-life exposure to toxicants exerts such persistent effects, the Toxicant Exposures and Responses by Genomic and Epigenomic Regulators of Transcription II (TaRGET II) Consortium generated a landmark resource comprising 2,570 epigenomes and 1,043 transcriptomes from longitudinal studies in mice. All data are publicly available through the TaRGET II data portal and the WashU Epigenome Browser. This resource from target (liver, brain, lung, heart) and surrogate (blood) tissues at weaning (3 weeks) and two adult time-points (5 and 10 months) characterized the molecular response to arsenic (As), lead (Pb), bisphenol-A (BPA), di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate(DEHP), tributyltin (TBT), tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD), and particulate matter with a diameter of <2.5μm (PM2.5). The findings revealed persistent, toxicant-specific, sex-dependent epigenomic and transcriptomic perturbations, resulting in disrupted expression of 14,908 genes, altered chromatin accessibility at 87,409 regulatory elements, DNA methylation changes at 113,186 genomic regions, and chromatin state switching of histone modifications. The resulting high-resolution map of how environmental exposures reprogram the epigenome and transcriptome is broadly accessible via ToxiTaRGET database, offering unparalleled opportunities for the scientific community to investigate the molecular underpinnings of environmental toxicant exposures and their contributions to disease pathogenesis.

observations.title: Toxicogenomic Insights into Environmental Toxicant Exposures: The TaRGET II Resource

observations.text: Dissociated neural cultures are living systems with no evolutionary history in their current form, which makes them a testbed for asking what goals neural tissue can learn to pursue once it is removed from its evolved body. It remains unclear which features of network activity such a culture can be trained to control, and whether that training is retained from one day to the next. We built an open-source closed-loop platform, the Holistic Agential Learning platform (HAL), that detects a network burst on a high-density microelectrode array, estimates its spatial origin in real time, and applies a minimal reinforcement rule. Here, a burst that originates off the goal side triggers global random stimulation that persists until the next burst. Over days of training, rat cortical cultures (n=10) increased the fraction of bursts that initiated on the goal side. This gain accrued between sessions, with little change within a session, a consolidation-like pattern that we interpret as a statement about timescale while the mechanism remains untested. The burst origin moved toward the goal side, while the burst peak and the repertoire of propagation directions were preserved. Trained cultures also recovered from incorrect states more reliably over days, while the rate at which they entered those states was unchanged, and this recovery effect was the most robust difference from unstimulated controls (n=6). Cultures that began on either side of chance converged to a similar level of performance. Damaged cultures (n=6) with comparable burst statistics showed neither the across-day gain nor the consolidation-like pattern. Training reweighted the activity patterns each culture already had, and we saw no new ones, which we read as a simple form of niche construction in which the tissue keeps a trace of its history that biases what it does next. These results identify burst initiation and error recovery as trainable variables in a novel living system, and they support training the tissue rather than engineering the machine.
observations.title: Goal directed closed-loop training of network bursts in cortical cultures produces improved performance and error correction over days

metadata.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked fatal disorder caused by dystrophin deficiency, characterized by early-onset, progressive degeneration of skeletal and cardiac muscle. Although microdystrophin (µDys) gene therapies provide functional benefit and partially restore tissue architecture, their impact on disease-associated cellular programs remains unclear. We evaluated proprietary codon-optimized µDys delivered via AAV8 under the MHCK7 promoter and a MyoD enhancer in severe DMD rats with an exon 52 deletion (DMDdel52). Therapy achieved sustained µDys expression with 90-97% of myofibers and cardiomyocytes, with proteins levels ranging from physiological to supra-physiological. Treatment preserved muscle function and extended survival beyond the median lifespan of untreated DMDdel52 rats, maintaining ambulation, climbing, weight gain, and muscle strength. Treatment also preserved cardiac architecture and function while preventing myonecrosis and adverse remodeling, with no detectable toxicity despite high µDys expression. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed that µDys treatment prevented disease-associated inflammatory and fibrotic activation of fibro-adipogenic progenitors, preserved a pro-regenerative interstitial environment and muscle stem cell quiescence while preventing senescence marker expression. These findings indicate that early µDys gene therapy preserves muscle homeostasis, function, and lifespan by preventing disease-associated cellular programs from becoming established within the regenerative niche of DMD rats.

observations.title: Optimized microdystrophin gene therapy preserves muscle homeostasis and extends survival in DMDdel52 rats

metadata.summary: Truncating variants in desmoplakin (DSP) are a leading cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a severe heart muscle disease characterized by fibrosis and life-threatening arrhythmias. Desmoplakin anchors the junctions that hold heart muscle cells together to the internal cytoskeleton, enabling the heart to withstand the force of each contraction. No targeted therapy exists, and DSP is too large for conventional gene replacement. Here we show, in explanted human hearts and in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, that truncating DSP variants reduce desmoplakin RNA and protein, and that the resulting haploinsufficiency renders cardiomyocytes vulnerable to cell–cell adhesion failure under contractile stress, preceded by disruption of the cell membrane. Lowering contractile force with the myosin inhibitor mavacamten prevents this failure. Circumventing the size of DSP, CRISPR-based transcriptional activation of the endogenous gene restores desmoplakin expression and rescues adhesion. Haploinsufficiency is therefore the primary defect in DSP cardiomyopathy, and transcriptional activation offers a therapeutic strategy.

observations.text:
Background and AimsArtificial intelligence (AI) is applied to histological assessment in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but most approaches quantify features without considering anatomical location. We developed and evaluated PAIR-IBD (Perspectum AI Reading in IBD), an AI system quantifying inflammatory cell, crypt injury, and epithelial damage within mucosal compartments to distinguish histologically-defined active disease, remission, and inconclusive cases in ulcerative colitis (UC), in a single clinical network.

MethodsA deep-learning ensemble was trained on three IBD datasets to identify lymphocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils, and plasma cells, and segment crypts, lamina propria (LP), surface epithelium and muscularis mucosae. Inflammatory cell densities and crypt injury metrics (mucin depletion, solidity, roughness, branching, and abscesses) were quantified. PAIR-IBD outputs were compared between pathologist-defined active UC and histological remission, evaluated in discordant cases and correlated with manual grading.

ResultsCompared with Nancy remission, active biopsies showed 2.1-fold higher LP neutrophil, 5.3-fold higher crypt neutrophil and 1.2-fold higher LP lymphocyte density. Active UC showed increased mucin depletion, crypt branching, and crypt abscesses, with reduced crypt solidity (p<0.0001 for all). PAIR-IBD metrics correlated with manual pathology scores and global indices, strongest for mucin depletion, crypt neutrophils, crypt roughness and reduced crypt solidity (rs=0.50-0.73). Up to 89% of inconclusive biopsies aligned with histological remission-like profiles for individual metrics, particularly mucin depletion.

ConclusionPAIR-IBD provides spatially resolved, quantitative assessment of inflammation, epithelial injury and crypt architecture in UC, with potential to support the characterization of inconclusive histology, complement scoring and contribute to histological endpoint assessment in clinical trials, pending validation.

What is already known on this topicHistological remission is a key treatment target in ulcerative colitis (UC), but assessment relies on ordinal pathologist scoring systems (Nancy Index, Robarts Histopathological Index, Geboes Score) that are subject to inter-rater variability.

What this study addsWe developed and evaluated PAIR-IBD, an artificial intelligence system quantifying inflammatory cell populations, crypt injury and epithelial damage across mucosal compartments in a single clinical network cohort. PAIR-IBD distinguished pathologist-defined active UC from remission and showed that inconclusive biopsies display a mixed rather than uniformly active or remission-like histological profile.

How this study might affect research, practice or policyThese findings support further evaluation of PAIR-IBD as an adjunct to conventional histological scoring, with potential applications in clinical trial endpoint assessment and adjudication of discordant biopsies, pending external validation.
observations.title: Spatial AI quantification of inflammatory and architectural features differentiates pathologist-defined active ulcerative colitis from histological remission

metadata.summary: INTRODUCTION: Adipose tissue plays a significant role in metabolism with cross-organ communication through adipokines and hormones. Sex-hormones have a special influence over the distribution and function of adipose tissue which varies based on gender. Gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT) is prescribed widely among transgender patients but its long-term effect on metabolism is still unclear. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, we investigated the longitudinal effects of GAHT of uniform regimen among 24 hormone-naïve individuals on adipose tissue metabolism, body composition, and insulin sensitivity. Patients with diabetes and certain comorbidities or taking medications affecting glucose metabolism were excluded. Baseline and follow up assessments at 6 months and 12 months included clinical parameters such as blood pressure, weight, BMI and waist and hip circumference measurements, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) for body composition, fasting blood samples for sex hormone levels, metabolic and inflammatory markers, and abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue biopsies for histological and transcriptomic analyses. RESULTS: After one year of GAHT, transfemales showed expected changes in sex hormone level along with increase in body fat (MD - 4.4, p= 0.17); metabolic changes such as increased cardiac markers NT-proBNP (MD -18.04, p = 0.002), Galectin-3 (MD -10567.4, p = 9.41E-05) and decrease in alkaline phosphatase (MD 15.13, p = 0.0006), and certain ceramides such as lactosyl C24 (MD 193439.9, p = 0.03) and sphingosine- 1-phosphate (MD 533175.7, p = 0.04). In transmales, testosterone therapy led to reduced fat mass [total body fat (MD 5.01, P-value 0.02) and limb fat (MD 3183.18, p = 0.04)]; increased lean mass (MD -2184. 19, p = 0.50) with improvements in insulin sensitivity [HOMA-IR (MD 0.64, p = 0.05) and ADIPO-IR (MD 2.54, p = 0.01)] and adipose tissue metabolism evidenced by reduced fat cell size and favorable adipokine profile. RNA sequencing of adipose tissue revealed altered gene expression patterns with a shift toward reduced inflammation and improved metabolic function among transmales. CONCLUSION: These findings confirm some of the known effect of GAHT in previous studies while providing additional mechanistic insights into distinct metabolic and adipose tissue changes among transgender individuals; with transmales experiencing improved insulin sensitivity and favorable adipose tissue remodeling. This is the first study known to us with comprehensive and longitudinal data on metabolic impact of GAHT, emphasizing the need for individualized monitoring and risk management of underlying chronic disease among transgender population taking GAHT.

observations.title: Insulin Sensitivity improves after Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy (GAHT) in Transmales through changes in Adipose Tissue Metabolism

metadata.summary: Muscle LIM Protein (MLP) is a key component of the cardiomyocyte Z disc that is essential for sarcomere integrity and cardiac homeostasis.  Loss of MLP function results in (cardio)myopathy phenotypes in animal models and is associated with inherited cardiomyopathies in humans. Here, we identify MLP as an evolutionarily conserved non-canonical RNA-binding protein and uncover RNA binding as a previously unrecognized mechanism involved in its cytoskeletal association. Using enhanced RNA interactome capture together with complementary biochemical approaches, we demonstrate direct RNA binding by MLP and map two short RNA-binding motifs adjacent to its LIM domains. Disrupting these motifs markedly reduces RNA association, including residues associated with cardiomyopathies. Mechanistically, RNA is required for MLP’s interactions with cytoskeletal proteins, and for the formation of higher-order MLP-containing assemblies. Consistently, RNA-binding-deficient MLP mutants exhibit impaired interactions with cytoskeletal proteins and reduced cytoskeletal retention. Our findings reveal the importance of RNA binding for the formation of MLP assemblies, and support the emerging role of RNA as a co-factor in the organization of macromolecular complexes, with potential relevance to human disease.

observations.title: RNA binding by Muscle LIM Protein is critical for ist cytoskeletal association and impaired by mutation of disease-associated regions

observations.text: Engineering agronomically relevant traits in crops often requires changing a gene's activity in a specific tissue, developmental stage or environmental condition while preserving its roles in other contexts. Designing such selective changes requires predicting how cis-regulatory sequences are interpreted in different biological states, as the same edit can have different effects across contexts. Genomic models have made substantial progress in predicting gene expression from DNA sequence, yet sequence-only predictors do not receive an explicit description of biological states. We introduce CROP-1 (Context-aware Regulatory Output Prediction model), which combines DNA sequence with transcription factor binding motifs and measured expression to predict gene activity as a function of both sequence and regulatory state. On a held-out test set spanning six plant species, CROP-1 achieves a median per-gene Pearson correlation across contexts of 0.831, compared with 0.486 for its parameter-matched sequence-only counterpart, and 57-246% higher median correlations than three genomic foundation models fully fine-tuned on the same task. Prediction accuracy also improves with scale: increasing model capacity reduces validation error by 48%, while expanding training data to include more diverse biological contexts reduces it by 58%. We then use gradient-based sequence optimisation to translate a desired gene expression pattern into candidate edits of its cis-regulatory sequence, targeting up- or down-regulation in one context while preserving expression in others. In soybean and tomato, edit designs with 1-20 nucleotide substitutions produce strong predicted target responses and much smaller average changes across non-target contexts. By connecting scalable learning of sequence-state relationships to selective edit design, CROP-1 provides a computational foundation for controlling where, when and under which conditions endogenous crop genes are active.
observations.title: Scaling a context-aware genomic model for condition-specific edit design in plants

observations.text: Rapid bacterial identification could help guide antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), but image-based classification must generalise across bacterial strains. We developed SC-MAPS, a multichannel microscopy dataset comprising 916,435 single cells from 13 bacterial species, with independent strains reserved for evaluation. Combining phase-contrast and fluorescence information using deep learning achieved 65.4% single-cell species-classification accuracy on held-out strains. To assess whether imperfect species predictions retained useful information for downstream testing, we defined eight antimicrobial-resistance-informed AST-routing groups. Pooling species probabilities increased routing accuracy to 77.1%, rising to 91.1% when predictions from five cells were combined and 96.2% with 20 cells. Synthetic mixtures revealed limitations in minority-species recovery, while exploratory analysis of unseen organisms demonstrated the potential for out-of-distribution detection. SC-MAPS provides a framework for investigating transferable bacterial phenotypes and developing image-based identification and AST-routing strategies.
observations.title: SC-MAPS: Image-based deep learning for bacterial identification and antibiotic-susceptibility testing

observations.text: Brain-state-guided and closed-loop transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) protocols have emerged as methods for decreasing the outcome variability and increasing the therapeutic effectiveness of stimulation protocols. However, existing brain-state-dependent TMS systems control only stimulation timing, while the location is fixed and manually adjusted between blocks or sessions. This limits targeting distributed cortical networks in a flexible brain-state-dependent paradigm. We developed a method that jointly manages TMS pulse timing and location automatically controlled by electroencephalography (EEG)-derived brain state. A machine-learning algorithm infers the brain state in real time to guide robotic coil placement. We present a proof-of-concept study in which EEG controlled both the target site and the timing of TMS. A pre-trained convolutional neural network discriminated between resting state and movements performed with the right or left hand; the classifier output determined the hemisphere in which primary-motor-cortex hand area was stimulated. Preprocessing and decoding of 2-s EEG segments required 150 ms, and the robot took 7.5 s to move from the vertex home position to the predefined motor targets. The EEG-guided robotic TMS method expands the toolkit for brain-state-dependent neurostimulation by enabling closed-loop control of stimulus location based on EEG-derived brain states, including volitional activity. Thus, the method can benefit both neuroscience research and clinical neuromodulation applications, such as by optimizing stimulation parameters to the brain state that produces optimal rehabilitation outcomes in spinal cord injury or motor disorders.
observations.title: EEG-guided robotic control of transcranial magnetic stimulation
